title: Bryophyta — Liverworts, Hornworts and Mosses
topicTitle: Bryophyta: General introduction and characteristic features of liverworts, hornworts and moss; morphological structure and reproduction of Marchantia; economic importance of bryophytes
notes: **General features of Bryophyta:** Non-vascular plants (no true xylem or phloem), dominant gametophyte generation (haploid, n, is the visible green plant), sporophyte (diploid, 2n) is attached to and nutritionally dependent on the gametophyte, require water for fertilisation because antherozoids are flagellated and must swim to archegonia, embryo develops protected within the archegonium (hence 'embryophytes'), rhizoids (root-like filaments) for anchorage only — no water/nutrient conduction, cell walls of cellulose, store food as starch. Called 'amphibians of the plant kingdom' because they require a film of water for sexual reproduction, just as amphibian animals require water for reproduction.

**Classification of Bryophyta into three classes:** Hepaticopsida (liverworts) — ~9,000 species, thalloid or leafy body, unicellular smooth rhizoids, oil bodies in cells. Anthocerotopsida (hornworts) — ~300 species, thalloid body with mucilage clefts harbouring Nostoc, sporophyte with basal meristem for indefinite growth, pseudo-elaters in sporangium. Bryopsida (mosses) — ~12,000 species, leafy gametophyte with phyllids on stem-like axis, multicellular rhizoids with oblique septa, protonema stage, peristome teeth on capsule. Together bryophytes comprise approximately 23,000 described species worldwide.

**Hepaticopsida (liverworts) — body forms:** Thalloid liverworts (Marchantia, Riccia, Pellia) — flattened, ribbon-like body with dorsal and ventral surfaces, no true stems or leaves. Leafy liverworts (Porella, Lepidozia, Radula) — small leaves in two or three rows on a stem-like axis, dorsiventral symmetry. Marchantia is dioecious (separate male and female plants); Riccia is monoecious (both sexes on same thallus). Liverwort oil bodies (membrane-bound organelles containing terpenoids) are unique to liverworts and may deter herbivory.

**Marchantia — morphological structure:** Dorsiventral thallus (2-10 cm wide, 0.5 mm thick), green, branching, attached to substrate by rhizoids. Dorsal surface: waxy epidermis with simple pores (not stomata — pores lack guard cells and do not open/close), air chambers below pores containing photosynthetic filaments, gemma cups on fertile thalli, midrib (thicker central region). Ventral surface: smooth scales (purple/black, protect against desiccation), unicellular smooth-walled rhizoids (anchorage and limited absorption), stored food as starch. The thallus grows from a marginal meristem at each branch tip.

**Marchantia — sexual reproduction (male):** Male (androecious) thalli produce antheridiophores — erect stalks (5-15 mm tall) with a disc-shaped head supported by 8-12 radiating rays (resembling an inverted umbrella or 'sun-tab'). Beneath each ray, a layer of sterile cells (paraphyses) protects the antheridia. Each antheridium is a flask-shaped structure with a sterile jacket wall surrounding spermatogenous tissue. When mature, the antheridium wall dissolves, releasing biflagellate antherozoids (sperm) into a film of water. Antherozoids swim to archegonia on female plants.

**Marchantia — sexual reproduction (female):** Female (gynoecious) thalli produce archegoniophores — erect stalks with 5-10 lobed, finger-like rays radiating downward (resembling a star or palm frond). Each ray bears 6-12 archegonia on its underside. Each archegonium is a flask-shaped structure with a neck (neck canal cell, venter canal cell), a swollen venter containing a single egg cell, and a jacket of sterile cells. After fertilisation, the archegoniophore rays curl inward, protecting the developing sporophyte from desiccation.

**Marchantia — sexual reproduction (zygote to sporophyte):** Fertilisation requires water — antherozoids swim from antheridiophore to archegoniophore. Zygote (2n) forms in the archegonial venter → divides by mitosis → embryo → sporophyte. The mature sporophyte is embedded in the archegoniophore and consists of: foot (absorbs nutrients from gametophyte), short seta (stalk), and capsule (sporangium). Inside the capsule, sporogenous tissue undergoes meiosis to produce haploid (n) spores. Elaters (sterile, hygroscopic cells with spiral thickenings) assist spore dispersal by twisting in response to humidity changes.

**Marchantia — asexual reproduction:** Gemma cups are small, cup-shaped structures on the dorsal surface of fertile thalli. Each cup contains several gemmae — lens-shaped, green, multicellular buds with a visible notch (the growing point). Gemmae are dispersed by raindrops splashing into the cup. Each gemma lands on moist substrate, the notch grows into a new thallus, and the original gemma degrades. This is a form of vegetative propagation that produces genetically identical clones. In dry seasons, Marchantia forms tubers (swollen thallus segments) that survive desiccation and germinate when moisture returns.

**Anthocerotopsida (hornworts) — distinctive features:** Gametophyte is a simple, lobed green thallus (resembling liverworts) but with important differences. Sporophyte is elongated, horn-like, and grows continuously from a basal meristem (intercalary meristem at the junction with the gametophyte) — this is unique among bryophytes. The sporophyte has a central columella (sterile tissue) surrounded by sporogenous tissue that produces spores and pseudo-elaters. Stomata are present on the sporophyte (unusual for bryophytes — their function is debated). Nostoc (cyanobacteria) colonies in mucilage clefts fix atmospheric nitrogen, providing the plant with usable nitrogen compounds.

**Bryopsida (mosses) — life cycle and structure:** Spores germinate into a filamentous, branched, photosynthetic protonema (resembling green algae) — this is the juvenile gametophyte stage. Buds on the protonema develop into the adult leafy gametophyte, which consists of a stem-like axis bearing spirally arranged leaf-like structures (phyllids — usually one cell thick). Rhizoids are multicellular with oblique (diagonal) septa. The sporophyte consists of a foot, a long seta (stalk that elevates the capsule), and a capsule with a operculum (lid) and peristome teeth (8-64 teeth made of overlapping translucent plates). Peristome teeth respond to humidity changes, opening when dry to release spores and closing when moist to prevent premature dispersal.

**Funaria — common moss life cycle:** Spores (n) germinate on damp soil → protonema (filamentous, transient stage) → buds form → adult gametophyte (leafy, with antheridia at stem tips and archegonia in axils of upper leaves) → water required for antherozoid swimming → zygote (2n) → embryo → sporophyte (seta elongates, pulling capsule upward — seta is positively phototropic) → capsule with operculum and peristome teeth → meiosis in sporogenous tissue → spores (n) released when operculum detaches. Funaria is commonly found on moist soil after forest fires, on rotten wood, and in acidic soils.

**Polytrichum — advanced moss features:** Often called 'hair-cap moss,' it is one of the tallest mosses (up to 50 cm). It has leaf-like structures with a midrib (costa) for support and oil cells between leaves. Rhizoids are multinucleate (multicellular). The capsule has a complex peristome with 40 teeth. Polytrichum has a cuticle (waxy layer) reducing water loss — unusual for mosses. It can tolerate drier conditions than most bryophytes and forms extensive carpets in forests. The sporophyte is ephemeral (short-lived) compared to the long-lived gametophyte.

**Sphagnum (peat moss) — unique adaptations:** Belongs to class Sphagnopsida (not Bryopsida). Leaves have two cell types: green photosynthetic cells (with chloroplasts) and large dead hyaline cells (with pores for water retention). Sphagnum can absorb 15-25 times its dry weight in water. Grows in acidic, nutrient-poor bogs where it outcompetes other plants by lowering pH (releasing H+ ions) and sequestering nutrients. Accumulates as peat — partially decayed organic matter. Peat formation rate: approximately 1 mm per year. Sphagnum-dominated peatlands cover ~3% of Earth's land surface but store ~30% of soil carbon — twice as much as all world forests combined.

**Economic importance of bryophytes:** (1) Peat (Sphagnum): fuel (peat fires), soil conditioner (increases water retention and acidity), packing material for live plants (holds water), historically used as wound dressings (antibacterial). (2) Soil formation: pioneer colonisers of bare rock, secrete organic acids that weather rock surfaces, build soil for other plants. (3) Water retention: moss carpets in forests hold rainfall, reduce runoff and soil erosion, maintain humidity. (4) Pollution indicators: mosses like Hypnum cupressiforme accumulate heavy metals from air — used as bioindicators of air quality. (5) Medicinal: some liverworts produce volatile oils with antimicrobial properties; Sphagnum's antibacterial properties were used in WWI wound dressings. (6) Ornamental: preserved moss arrangements, floral arrangements, terrariums.

**Why bryophytes are evolutionarily significant:** Bryophytes represent the transition from aquatic algae to terrestrial plants. Like algae: dominant gametophyte, no vascular tissue, flagellated sperm requiring water for fertilisation. Like pteridophytes: multicellular sex organs (antheridia and archegonia with sterile jacket cells), alternation of generations, diploid sporophyte embryo, sporopollenin in spore walls. Unlike both: rhizoids instead of true roots, no true leaves, sporophyte permanently attached to and nutritionally dependent on gametophyte. This intermediate position makes bryophytes critical for understanding plant terrestrialisation (~470 million years ago, Ordovician period).

**Ecological roles of bryophytes:** Moisture retention — moss carpets can absorb rainfall equal to 5-10 times their weight, reducing soil erosion and maintaining microclimate humidity. Carbon sequestration — Sphagnum peatlands store more carbon than all world forests combined. Habitat provision — bryophyte mats provide microhabitats for invertebrates, amphibians, and soil microbes. Nutrient cycling — Nostoc symbiosis in hornworts fixes atmospheric nitrogen. Pioneer species — bryophytes colonise bare rock, weather it, and create conditions for vascular plants to establish. In Nepal, bryophytes are abundant in high-altitude forests, along stream banks, and on moist rock faces throughout the Himalayas.
confusion:
❌ Bryophytes have true roots.
✅ Bryophytes have rhizoids — simple filamentous structures for anchorage only. Liverwort rhizoids are unicellular and smooth-walled; moss rhizoids are multicellular with oblique (diagonal) septa. Rhizoids lack xylem and phloem, cannot conduct water internally, and are single-layered. True roots (found in pteridophytes and higher plants) have vascular tissue, root caps, root hairs, and branched structures for water and mineral absorption.

❌ Bryophytes do not need water for reproduction.
✅ Bryophytes REQUIRE water for sexual reproduction. Antherozoids (male gametes) are biflagellated and must swim through a film of water to reach the archegonium (female organ). Without water, fertilisation cannot occur, and the sporophyte generation cannot be produced. This is why bryophytes are restricted to moist habitats and are called 'amphibians of the plant kingdom' — just as amphibians need water for reproduction, so do bryophytes.

❌ Sphagnum and Funaria are in the same class of mosses.
✅ Sphagnum belongs to class Sphagnopsida (peat mosses) with unique features: leaves with two cell types (photosynthetic + hyaline), no chlorophyll in rhizoids, peristome teeth absent (spores released through cap). Funaria belongs to class Bryopsida (true mosses) with typical moss features: one-cell-thick leaves, chlorophyllous rhizoids, complex peristome with 40 teeth. They are both bryophytes but in different classes with distinct morphology and ecology.

❌ Hornwort sporophytes are the same as liverwort or moss sporophytes.
✅ Hornwort sporophytes grow continuously from a basal meristem (intercalary growth) throughout their life — they never stop growing. Liverwort sporophytes are sessile (no seta) and grow to a fixed size. Moss sporophytes grow to a fixed height on a seta that elongates from the base during development, then stops. The hornwort's basal meristem is a unique feature among bryophytes, making their sporophytes qualitatively different.

❌ Peat is the same as coal.
✅ Peat is the earliest stage of coal formation — partially decayed plant matter (mainly Sphagnum) accumulated under waterlogged, anaerobic conditions. Peat has ~50% carbon content and can be used directly as fuel. Coal is formed from peat subjected to heat and pressure over millions of years (carbonisation). Anthracite coal has 86-97% carbon; bituminous coal has 60-80%. Peat extraction for fuel is controversial because peatlands store vast amounts of carbon — draining them releases CO2.

❌ Marchantia antheridiophore and archegoniophore look the same.
✅ They are morphologically distinct: antheridiophore (male) has flat, disc-shaped tips on radiating rays — resembling an umbrella handle or 'sun-tab' from above. Archegoniophore (female) has lobed, finger-like rays curving downward — resembling a star, palm frond, or 'umbrella turned inside out' from below. The archegonia hang from the underside of each ray. Mistaking them is common in practical exams — remember: male = flat disc (sun-tab), female = hanging lobes (star).

❌ Bryophyte spores are gametes that fuse to form a zygote.
✅ Bryophyte spores are haploid (n) cells produced by meiosis in the sporophyte capsule — they are NOT gametes. Spores germinate to produce a new gametophyte generation. The actual gametes are the antherozoids (sperm, produced by antheridia on the gametophyte) and the egg cell (produced by archegonia on the gametophyte). Fertilisation = fusion of antherozoid + egg → diploid zygote (2n). This is the key distinction: spores start a new generation; gametes fuse to form the next generation.

❌ Bryophytes are ferns (pteridophytes).
✅ Bryophytes and pteridophytes are distinct plant divisions. Bryophytes: non-vascular, dominant gametophyte, no true roots/stems/leaves, require water for fertilisation, sporophyte dependent on gametophyte. Pteridophytes (ferns): vascular (xylem and phloem), dominant sporophyte, true roots/stems/leaves, still require water for fertilisation but sporophyte is independent. Ferns can grow tall (due to vascular tissue); bryophytes remain low-growing (max a few cm). Bryophytes appeared ~470 MYA; pteridophytes ~420 MYA.
practice: **Q1:** Why are bryophytes called the 'amphibians of the plant kingdom'? *Solution:* Like amphibians (animals) that require water for reproduction (eggs laid in water, larval stage aquatic), bryophytes require a film of water for fertilisation. Antherozoids are flagellated and must swim through water to reach archegonia. Without water, the male gamete cannot reach the female gamete, and no zygote forms. This water dependency restricts bryophytes to moist habitats and prevents them from colonising dry environments, just as amphibians are constrained by their reproductive water requirement.

**Q2:** Differentiate between liverworts and mosses with respect to rhizoids and gametophyte structure. *Solution:* Liverworts: (a) Rhizoids are unicellular and smooth-walled — each rhizoid is a single elongated cell. (b) Gametophyte is either thalloid (flat, ribbon-like, dorsiventral — e.g., Marchantia) or leafy (small leaves in 2-3 rows on a stem-like axis — e.g., Porella). Mosses: (a) Rhizoids are multicellular with oblique (diagonal) septa — each rhizoid is a filament of multiple cells. (b) Gametophyte is leafy — clearly differentiated stem-like axis with spirally arranged leaf-like phyllids (one cell layer thick), often with a midrib (costa). The protonema stage (filamentous juvenile) precedes the leafy adult in mosses but is absent in liverworts.

**Q3:** Draw and label the structure of a Marchantia gemma cup. *Solution:* The gemma cup is a small, cup-shaped depression on the dorsal (upper) surface of the thallus, typically 1-2 mm in diameter. The cup wall is formed by raised thallus tissue. Inside the cup, the floor is lined with photosynthetic parenchyma cells. Gemmae are lens-shaped (biconvex), green, multicellular structures scattered on the cup floor. Each gemma has a visible median notch — this is the growing point where cell division will produce a new thallus after detachment. Rain splash is the dispersal mechanism: a raindrop hits the cup, splashes gemmae out. Each detached gemma lands on moist soil, the notch grows into a new thallus, and the rest of the gemma degenerates. Label: cup wall, gemma, growing point (notch), photosynthetic floor cells.

**Q4:** Describe the life cycle of Funaria (moss) with labelled stages. *Solution:* Stage 1: Spore (n) lands on moist substrate. Stage 2: Spore germinates → produces a filamentous, branched, green protonema (transient juvenile stage, photosynthetic). Stage 3: Buds form on protonema → each bud develops into an adult leafy gametophyte (stem-like axis with spirally arranged phyllids, rhizoids on underside). Stage 4: Gametophyte matures → antheridia form at stem tips (male), archegonia form in leaf axils (female). Stage 5: Water enters → antherozoids (biflagellate sperm) swim from antheridium to archegonium. Stage 6: Fertilisation → zygote (2n) forms in archegonial venter. Stage 7: Zygote → embryo → sporophyte (foot embedded in gametophyte, elongating seta, capsule at apex). Stage 8: Meiosis in capsule → spores (n) formed. Stage 9: Operculum detaches, peristome teeth open in dry conditions → spores released. The dominant, visible phase is the gametophyte; the sporophyte is dependent and short-lived.

**Q5:** What is the economic importance of Sphagnum? *Solution:* (1) Peat fuel — Sphagnum accumulated as peat is dried and burned as fuel; peat fires provide heat and cooking energy in rural Ireland, Scotland, and parts of Scandinavia. (2) Packing material — Sphagnum holds 15-25× its weight in water and is sterile; used to pack live plants for shipping because it keeps roots moist without rotting. (3) Soil conditioner — mixing Sphagnum peat into garden soil increases water retention in sandy soils and improves drainage in clay soils; it also acidifies soil (pH 3.5-4.5), ideal for ericaceous plants (rhododendrons, blueberries). (4) Historical wound dressings — Sphagnum's antibacterial properties (hydrogen peroxide production, low pH, high osmotic pressure) made it the preferred wound dressing in WWI; it was more effective than boiled cotton. (5) Carbon storage — Sphagnum peatlands store ~30% of global soil carbon; their preservation is critical for climate change mitigation.

**Q6:** Differentiate between antheridiophore and archegoniophore of Marchantia. *Solution:* ANtheridiophore (male reproductive structure): (a) borne on male (androecious) thallus; (b) stalk is erect, topped by a flat, disc-shaped head (resembling an umbrella handle or 'sun-tab') supported by 8-12 radiating rays; (c) antheridia line the underside of each ray segment, protected by paraphyses; (d) produces biflagellate antherozoids. ARchegoniophore (female reproductive structure): (a) borne on female (gynoecious) thallus; (b) stalk is erect, with 5-10 lobed, finger-like rays radiating downward (resembling a star or palm frond); (c) archegonia hang from the underside of each ray, each with a neck and swollen venter containing an egg; (d) after fertilisation, rays curl inward to protect the developing sporophyte. Key visual distinction: male = flat disc (sun), female = hanging lobes (star).

**Q7:** Explain why the sporophyte of bryophytes is nutritionally dependent on the gametophyte, unlike pteridophytes. *Solution:* In bryophytes, the sporophyte lacks vascular tissue (no xylem/phloem) and cannot photosynthesise efficiently (limited chlorophyll in capsule). The foot (basal region) of the sporophyte is embedded in the gametophyte tissue, absorbing water, minerals, and photosynthates (sugars) directly from the gametophyte. The seta simply elevates the capsule. In contrast, pteridophyte sporophytes have true vascular tissue (xylem with tracheids, phloem with sieve tubes), true roots that absorb from soil, and photosynthetic leaves — making them fully independent. The bryophyte sporophyte's dependence is an evolutionary primitive trait reflecting the transition from aquatic to terrestrial life.
universalFacts: Bryophytes were the first plants to colonise land over 470 million years ago (Ordovician period) — moss-like fossils called 'liverworts' appear in the fossil record before any other land plants.
The word 'liverwort' originates from medieval herbal medicine — liverworts were believed to treat liver diseases because their thallus resembled a liver shape.
Sphagnum peat bogs are the oldest ecosystems in northern Europe — some are over 10,000 years old, and individual bog surfaces advance at only 1 metre per year.
Bryophytes can survive extreme dehydration — many mosses can lose up to 90% of their water content and revive within hours of rehydration, a phenomenon called desiccation tolerance.
Marchantia polymorpha was the first plant on which the sex chromosomes were discovered — it has separate male and female plants (dioecious), with sex determined by U and V chromosomes.
